title: Officer involved in Elmvale mall fatal shooting previously charged by SIU
article: One of the officers involved in the shooting death of an axe-wielding man at Elmvale mall Thursday morning has faced the scrutiny of police oversight before, the other is a junior officer who was hired in 2016, this newspaper has learned.

Ottawa police responded to a report of a man, dressed all in black, wearing a hat with the word "Dope" written on it, carrying a weapon at the Elmvale Acres Shopping Centre at 1922 St. Laurent Blvd. just before 8 a.m. Thursday.
The man has since been identified by those who knew him as Greg Ritchie, a 30-year-old Indigenous man who'd recently moved to Ottawa from the Kitchener area.

Constables Thanh Tran and Daniel Vincelette were the first responding officers. Within minutes they had located Ritchie, armed with a small axe, whose actions led at least one person to call police reporting his behaviour. A confrontation ensued.

The officers attempted to deploy a Taser - or, conducted energy weapon - to subdue Ritchie, but sources say he continued to advance on the officers with the axe still in hand. At some point, Vincelette was slashed on the forehead.
It's believed both officers fired their guns, but it's unknown if bullets from both weapons hit Ritchie, who was shot multiple times.

He was without vital signs after the shooting. Both officers on scene and OC Transpo special constables nearby began efforts to revive him. He was transported to the trauma centre where he was officially pronounced dead.

The Special Investigations Unit, the province's civilian police watchdog, is now investigating the fatal shooting: the third by an Ottawa officer in three years, the fourth police-involved death in four years.

The incident comes as emotions are high both in the force and in the community as the much anticipated manslaughter trial of Const. Daniel Montsion is set to begin on Monday. Montsion, an anti-gang officer, was charged for the in-custody death of 37-year-old Somali man Abdirahman Abdi in 2016. Abdi died on the steps of his Hintonburg apartment building, handcuffed and bleeding. His family alleged excessive force, the community alleged racism and police officers maintained that Montsion was doing his job to subdue a man who'd allegedly assaulted women at a nearby coffee shop.

Tran, with more than a decade of policing experience, knows well the process of police oversight. Along with another officer, he was charged with assaulting a man sleeping on a Sandy Hill sidewalk in 2011, after that man was taken to hospital with facial fractures. Tran and the other officer were accused of tripping and pushing the man face first onto the pavement around 5:30 a.m. on Aug. 13, 2011 after rousing him from sleep next to two empty bottles of Listerine.
A trial in 2013 led to acquittals on all criminal charges for both Tran and the other officer.
The judge ultimately found that the officers made an appropriate "split-second decision" and responded with necessary force to subdue a tall, drunk man waving his arms aggressively in the street.

The trial was marked by what the judge called the inconsistent and unreliable testimony of key witnesses who saw the alleged beating and first reported it to this newspaper rather than to authorities. The judge said they prioritized media interviews over meeting with investigators on the case.
Tran faced no internal discipline and a $500,000 lawsuit filed by the complainant was later dropped. Though he was placed on administrative duties after he was charged, he later returned to the road.

Vincelette, a second-generation police officer whose father worked as an Ottawa police officer, was hired by the force in August 2016. He worked as a dispatcher for the police service before being sworn in as an officer and has spent his career, to date, as a patrol officer responding to calls for service.
Officers who know both men called them capable and well respected.

Though the officers are believed to have deployed a taser, others warn that in the winter months tasers are harder to deploy. In order to subdue someone, both prongs fired from a taser have to get close to a person's skin. That is harder to achieve when people are wearing thick clothing or multiple layers.
When reached for comment through their police association, union president Matt Skof would not comment on the identities of the officers but said both await a thorough investigation.
The shooting is the city's second homicide of 2019.

Fatal police-involved shootings are homicides - they are events in which people have been killed, but they are not necessarily considered a crime. A police officer may use lethal force in the course of their job and the SIU will determine if instances of lethal force are lawful, justified killings or criminal acts.
The SIU found Ottawa police's 2017 fatal shooting of a homicide suspect in the ByWard Market who was firing his gun at a police officer to be justified.
A 2018 fatal shooting of a man with a knife who fled a grocery store after stabbing two people is still under SIU investigation.
